title: The Holy Spirit
lead: The Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma both mean breath, wind and spirit. From creation to the church, the Spirit of God gives life, power, prophecy and holiness.

sections.b: "God's Spirit fluttered over the face of the waters" (Genesis 1:2); the word for Spirit is ruach. The Spirit came on judges, kings and prophets for particular tasks (Judges 6:34; 1 Samuel 16:13), and the prophets promised a day when God would put his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28–29).
sections.refs: Genesis 1:2; Judges 6:34; 1 Samuel 16:13; Psalms 51:11; Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28–29

sections.b: Jesus promised "another Helper" (John 14:16–17). At Pentecost the Spirit was poured out on all believers (Acts 2). Paul says "if someone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person is not his" (Romans 8:9), and that the Spirit helps us pray (Romans 8:26–27). The KJV's "Holy Ghost" is the same phrase; "ghost" then meant "spirit."
sections.refs: John 14:16–17; Acts 2:1–4; Romans 8:9–16; Romans 8:26–27; 1 Corinthians 2:10–16; Galatians 5:22–25

sections.h: How Jews and Christians understand the Spirit
sections.b: In the Hebrew Bible and in Jewish tradition, ruach ha-qodesh, "the holy spirit," is God's own presence and power at work, especially in prophecy, not a separate person; rabbinic texts often say the holy spirit "rested on" a prophet or sage. Christians came to confess the Spirit as a distinct person of the one God: the Council of Constantinople (AD 381) called the Spirit "the Lord, the giver of life," worshiped with the Father and the Son. Eastern and Western churches later divided over the filioque ("and the Son"), the Western addition saying the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Some modern Christian groups, such as Jehovah's Witnesses, regard the Spirit as God's active force rather than a person.
